subtype: Laws as agreements that serve people [Actor]
passage:
Debate society log, Gandhi Jayanti week. Shankar (coach)
Mock parliament today on the new hostel rule that bars students from the library after 9 pm. Most speakers split into two camps: rules are rules, obey; or just sneak in, who cares.
Sachin took neither side. He said the rule exists to protect people, since the library had two thefts late at night, so it is not pointless. But it also harms students with day jobs who can only study at night. "If a rule stops serving the people it's meant for, we don't break it and we don't just suffer it. We change it." He proposed a signed petition to the dean and a trial of ID-card entry till midnight.
I asked him to draft the petition with the hostel committee. He meets them on Monday.

qa.q: How many thefts had the library had late at night?
qa.a: Two thefts.

qa.q: How does Sachin seem to feel about the library rule?
qa.a: Sachin seems thoughtful and fair-minded, accepting that the rule has a real purpose but frustrated that it harms students with day jobs, so he wants it changed properly.

qa.q: Why is Sachin's approach stronger than obeying blindly or sneaking in?
qa.a: It respects why the rule exists but uses fair means, a petition and a trial of ID-card entry, to fix the harm, so the change lasts and includes everyone.

qa.q: How might a student with a day job feel hearing Sachin's speech?
qa.a: They would likely feel seen and hopeful, since someone named their problem and proposed a fair fix instead of telling them to break or suffer the rule.

grounding: A coach notes a student arguing that a rule should protect people and that an unfair one should be changed by petition.

passage:
The Dussehra week the new timetable came out, I almost signed it without reading, like always. I'm a scheduler at the city bus depot, and ninety-nine times out of a hundred, the rule is the rule and I follow it. But route 47's last bus, the 11:15 past the nurses' hostel, had been cut to save fuel. I thought of the nurses finishing late shifts and walking that dark road.
So I did it properly. I wrote to the depot committee with the ridership numbers and the night-shift timings, and asked for a hearing. Arohi from planning helped me with the figures.
The committee listened, and still kept the cut. They added a hospital shuttle till midnight instead. It wasn't what I asked for. But they heard it, and gave reasons. I signed. Ojas the troublemaker, they call me now, but kindly.

qa.q: What time was route 47's last bus?
qa.a: The 11:15, past the nurses' hostel.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel about the committee's final decision?
qa.a: Ojas felt disappointed that the cut stayed but respected the fair hearing and the reasons, so accepted it and signed.

qa.q: Which choices made Ojas's objection work within the system?
qa.a: Writing to the committee with ridership numbers and shift timings, asking for a hearing, and then accepting the outcome of that process.

qa.q: How might the nurses on late shifts see the hospital shuttle?
qa.a: They might feel relieved to have a safe ride till midnight, even though the bus itself was cut.

grounding: A professional follows rules in ordinary cases but formally objects to a bus cut, then accepts the committee's reasoned decision.

subtype: Person affected by a fair process feels respected [Receiver]
passage:
The office basement had flooded in the first heavy monsoon week, so Manoj's review meeting was squeezed into the pantry, the coffee machine gurgling beside them.
Three weeks earlier he had filed a complaint: the team lead post had gone to a newer colleague, and he felt skipped. Nandini from HR laid the file on the table. The three criteria, the panel's scores, the notes from both interviews, his own comments, all there.
"We went through it again, openly," she said. "The decision stands. Her client work scored higher. Here's where you lost points, and here's a plan so you're ready next cycle."
Manoj read every page. It stung. But nobody had brushed him off or talked down to him.
"Thank you for actually explaining," he said, and meant it. Walking out under the dripping ceiling, he felt oddly steady.

qa.q: Where was Manoj's review meeting held?
qa.a: In the pantry, because the basement had flooded.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel after reading the file?
qa.a: It stung, but he felt respected and oddly steady, because nobody brushed him off and every score came with a reason.

qa.q: What made the process feel fair even though the result went against Manoj?
qa.a: The criteria, scores and notes were shown openly, the decision was explained, and a plan was offered for the next cycle.

qa.q: What would change if Nandini had just said the decision was final?
qa.a: Manoj would likely have felt dismissed and bitter, and trusted the system less, even with the same result.

grounding: An employee whose complaint is reviewed openly and answered with reasons feels respected despite losing.

passage:
The staff meeting at the girls' school in Lucknow was nearly over when the principal read out the new rule: any student more than five minutes late would be sent home for the day.
Parveen, in her second year of teaching, watched Salma raise her hand. Salma had been at the school twelve years and never missed a single duty.
"Ma'am, I support punctuality," Salma said evenly. "But forty of our girls come on the village bus, and it runs late three days a week. I've listed the dates. I'd like to request, in writing, a separate gate register for bus students."
Nobody laughed. Nobody rolled their eyes. The principal took the paper and said the committee would review it on Friday.
Parveen felt something shift. She had thought you either obeyed rules or grumbled in the corridor. Salma had done neither.

qa.q: How many of the girls come on the village bus?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: What did Parveen feel as Salma spoke?
qa.a: Parveen felt surprised and admiring, seeing a way between obeying silently and grumbling in the corridor.

qa.q: Which parts of Salma's objection made it principled rather than rebellious?
qa.a: She said she supported punctuality, brought the dates as evidence, and made a written request through the committee instead of sneering at or ignoring the rule.

qa.q: How might Salma see her own role at the school?
qa.a: Salma likely sees herself as loyal to the school, never missing a duty, and speaking up because she cares about its students, not to oppose it.

grounding: A young teacher watches a senior colleague object to an unfair rule through proper channels and learns that loyalty and principle can go together.

passage:
Naveen tapped the register. "Okay. The rule says no pets in the lift. Mrs Irawati Sen on the ninth floor has a dog and a bad knee. Let's hear everyone before anyone decides."
"Rules are rules," said Mr Kapadia. "My granddaughter is scared of dogs."
"That matters," Naveen said. "Her safety and comfort count. Irawati-ji?"
"I can't do nine floors of stairs," Irawati said quietly. "Not twice a day. I'm not asking for favours. Just a way to keep living here."
"That matters too," Naveen said. "So we have two real needs. The bye-laws say any change needs a general body vote. Until then, how about this: pets use the service lift, on a leash, with a sign so families know."
Mr Kapadia paused. "The service lift. Fine. Until the vote."
"I'll draft the amendment tonight," Naveen said.

qa.q: Which floor does Irawati live on?
qa.a: The ninth floor.

qa.q: How does Irawati seem to feel asking for a solution?
qa.a: She seems worried and a little embarrassed, saying quietly that she is not asking for favours, just a way to keep living there.

qa.q: What steps did Naveen take to handle the rule conflict fairly?
qa.a: He heard everyone first, named both needs as real, checked the bye-laws requiring a vote, offered an interim service-lift fix and planned to draft an amendment.

qa.q: How might Mr Kapadia see the outcome?
qa.a: Mr Kapadia, worried for his granddaughter, may feel his concern was taken seriously, which is why he accepts the service lift until the vote.

grounding: An adult handles a housing society rule conflict by hearing both sides, following the bye-laws and drafting an amendment.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Chand raat. Sumit snatched Asif's green balloon. Asif's hand flew up, then stopped in the air. "No hitting," he said loudly. "Ammi will get angry."
Eid morning. Ammi, oiling his hair, asked, "Why is hitting wrong, Asif?"
"Because you get a scolding."
"And if nobody saw?"
Asif frowned hard. "Then... it's still a rule," he said, as if that settled it.
Two days later, his cousin smacked the cat. Asif gasped. "You'll get punished!"

qa.q: What did Sumit snatch?
qa.a: Asif's green balloon.

qa.q: Why did Asif stop his hand in the air?
qa.a: He was scared Ammi would get angry, so fear of a scolding, not Sumit's feelings, is what stopped him.

qa.q: How could Ammi help Asif grow beyond "you get a scolding"?
qa.a: Gently add a reason about feelings, like "Hitting hurts, and the cat felt scared too," while still praising him for stopping.

qa.q: How might the cousin feel when Asif shouts "You'll get punished!"?
qa.a: The cousin might feel scared or defensive, worried an adult will come, rather than thinking about the cat.

grounding: A young child sees hitting as wrong because it brings a scolding, and treats the rule as a plain fact.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
It was the last evening of the Onam holidays, and the gang had planned the late movie. Gurleen had already booked six seats. "Thomas, you're coming, right? You said you would."
At the same moment Mummy's text came: "Bring Ammachi home from the church hall at 8.30, mone. Papa is stuck at work."
The movie started at 8.15. Thomas stood at the bus stop in the drizzle, phone in both hands. If he skipped the movie, Gurleen would say he always ditched. If he skipped Ammachi, Mummy would be so disappointed, and he would hear about it from every aunty at Sunday Mass.
He typed "coming!" to the group, deleted it. Typed "sorry Mummy" and deleted that too.
"Why do I have to be the bad guy either way?" he muttered.

qa.q: What time did the movie start?
Why does Thomas type and delete both messages?
qa.a: He feels torn and anxious, wanting to be seen as a good friend by Gurleen and a good son by Mummy, and hating the idea of disappointing either.

qa.q: What would you advise Thomas to do?
qa.a: Pick up Ammachi as asked, and tell Gurleen honestly and early why, perhaps offering to join the gang afterwards or next time.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel if Thomas explains honestly?
qa.a: Gurleen may be disappointed about the booked seat but would likely understand a grandmother needing a ride, especially if told early.

grounding: A teenager torn between being a loyal friend and a good son dreads disappointing either side.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Dhanteras. As mess secretary, Rekha stopped a first-year at the door with a fistful of laddoos. "Food doesn't leave the mess. What if everyone did that?" He put them back.
Diwali night. Crackers outside, the mess half empty. Vikas came with a steel box. "Rekha, my roommate has fever, he can't come down. Let me take him dal-rice."
"A rule's a rule, Vikas. If I allow you, fifty people will want it tomorrow."
"He's sick."
"I'm sorry." She held the door.
Two days later Vikas mentioned that his roommate had gone to bed hungry that night. Rekha felt a knot in her stomach. She still believed the rule held the mess together. But that evening she wrote to the warden asking for an official sick-tray register.

qa.q: What did Vikas want to take to his roommate?
qa.a: Dal-rice in a steel box.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on hearing the roommate went to bed hungry?
qa.a: Rekha felt a knot of guilt and unease, though she still believed the rule held the mess together.

qa.q: What did Rekha do with that feeling, and why does it fit her way of thinking?
qa.a: She asked the warden for an official sick-tray register, making room for rare cases through a proper rule instead of bending it herself.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt on Diwali night?
qa.a: Vikas probably felt frustrated and let down, seeing a sick friend's need blocked by a rule applied without exception.

grounding: A young adult enforces a mess rule strictly, asking what if everyone broke it, and is hard on a sick student's rare need.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
passage:
Subject: A question about the Kohlberg unit

Dear Vasudha Ma'am,
Something from my practice-teaching week keeps coming back to me. In the class debate on Tuesday, Kiran from Class 11 argued brilliantly that laws should protect everyone's rights and be changed fairly when they fail. Textbook stage 5, I wrote in my notes.
Then on Thursday I heard the same Kiran tell a junior, "Don't cheat, you'll get caught." Pure punishment talk. And by Friday Kiran was defending a friend who had copied, because "friends stick together".
I nearly wrote "inconsistent" in my report. But I don't think Kiran is a stage. Kiran reasons differently depending on the pressure. I think I'd been using the stages to rank students, when they are really a way to watch reasoning grow.
Does that make sense?
Shreya

qa.q: What did Kiran tell a junior on Thursday?
qa.a: "Don't cheat, you'll get caught."

qa.q: Why did Shreya hold back from writing "inconsistent" in the report?
qa.a: Shreya felt uneasy about labelling Kiran, realising the stages had been used to rank students rather than to watch reasoning grow.

qa.q: How could Shreya use the stage model more wisely in the report?
qa.a: Describe the different kinds of reasoning Kiran used in each situation and what seemed to shape them, instead of assigning one stage or a judgement.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel if the report simply said "inconsistent"?
qa.a: Kiran might feel judged and confused, since the debate reasoning was strong, and could lose confidence rather than grow.

grounding: A trainee teacher notices a student reasoning at different levels in different situations and stops using the stages as ranks.

subtopic: Kohlberg stages: contrast with other stages
passage:
Last Christmas season the hotel in Goa was full to the roof, and the manager called me aside. "Yusuf, if guests from that one community come asking, say we're booked. Other guests complain." Yash, at the next counter, just nodded. Everyone did.
I couldn't. That night a family came in, tired kids asleep on their shoulders, and we had rooms. I gave them one. Next morning I told the manager, calmly, that I would not turn people away for who they are, and that he could write me up if he wanted.
He did. I lost my festival bonus and was moved to night shifts for two months. Yash said I was mad.
I'm not a saint. I've kept quiet about smaller things before, and probably will again. But that one, I couldn't carry.

qa.q: What did it cost Yusuf to give the family a room?
qa.a: Yusuf lost the festival bonus and was moved to night shifts for two months.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel about turning people away, and what shows it?
qa.a: Yusuf felt it was deeply wrong, something impossible to carry, so stayed calm and firm even knowing a write-up would follow.

qa.q: Which parts of Yusuf's response would you point out to someone facing an unfair instruction?
qa.a: Yusuf acted openly and calmly, told the manager directly, and accepted the consequences instead of hiding or lying about it.

qa.q: Why might Yash react differently?
qa.a: Yash, like everyone else, went along with the manager, perhaps valuing the job and the group's approval more, so Yusuf's stand looked mad to Yash.

grounding: An adult refuses a discriminatory instruction on principle, accepts the cost, and admits not always living up to it.
